title: The ENTIRE History of the Mongol Empire in 10 Minutes
youtube_title: The ENTIRE History of the Mongol Empire in 10 Minutes
description:
From an abandoned boy on the Mongolian steppe to the biggest connected land empire in history, this is the Mongol Empire from 1206 to 1368 in about ten minutes: Genghis Khan's rise, the Yam relay system and paiza passes, the conquest of Khwarazm, why the Mongols left Europe in 1242, the fall of Baghdad, the defeat at Ain Jalut, Kublai Khan's paper money, the kamikaze storms off Japan and the fall of the Yuan dynasty. Every fact is checked, and legends are labelled as legends.

Chapters are added automatically.

#history #mongolempire #genghiskhan #kublaikhan #animatedhistory

beats.say: Mongolia, the 1170s. A young boy and his family are left behind by their whole clan, alone on the freezing grassland.
They survive on roots, wild berries and whatever fish they can catch.
Nobody is coming to help us. So we help ourselves.
Good news, Mom. I caught a fish. A really, really small fish.
About a hundred years later, that boy's family ruled the biggest connected land empire in history.
About twenty-four million square kilometers. That's roughly the size of all of North America.

show.label: The Mongol Empire at its biggest
show.sub: about the size of North America

beats.say: So how did a starving kid's family grab a huge chunk of the world? And how did it all fall apart? Let's find out.

show.text: The ENTIRE History of the Mongol Empire in 10 Minutes

beats.say: The boy was named Temüjin, and he was born on the steppe, the endless grassland of Mongolia, probably in the 1160s.
Back then the Mongols weren't one nation. They were rival tribes that raided each other's horses and camps all the time.
When Temüjin was about nine, his father, a chief named Yesügei, was poisoned by enemies from the Tatar tribe.
His clan decided a widow with small kids was useless, and just rode away without them.
His mother, Hö'elün, kept the family alive through pure stubbornness, and taught her kids to stick together.
It got darker. As a teenager, Temüjin quarrelled with his older half-brother over food, and killed him.
Later a rival clan captured him and locked his neck in a heavy wooden collar. He escaped anyway.
As he grew up, he won followers in a new way: he promoted people for talent and loyalty, not for having a fancy family.
By 1206, after years of war, he'd united the tribes. A great meeting of chiefs, called a kurultai, gave him a new title: Genghis Khan.

show.label: THE GREAT MONGOL STATE
show.sub: 1206 · Genghis raised a white banner with nine tails

beats.say: Historians still argue about what 'Genghis' means. The usual guess is something like 'universal ruler'.

tag.text: Genghis Khan, ruler of the Mongols

beats.say: New rules, everybody. We're one people now. And I'm in charge.
Can we still steal each other's horses?
No.
He also started something clever: the Yam, a chain of relay stations with fresh horses, so riders could carry messages across the empire super fast.
Marco Polo, a traveler from Venice, later claimed the system used two hundred thousand horses.

show.label: Horses in the Yam, according to Marco Polo
show.sub: with a station about every 25 miles

beats.say: Official travelers carried a paiza, a tablet of wood or metal that proved who they were. Think of it as an early passport.
And religion? Genghis didn't make people switch gods. Buddhist, Christian, Muslim and Daoist clergy were even excused from taxes, as long as they prayed for the Khan.
Traders loved it too. With the Mongols guarding the Silk Road, the old trade routes between China and Europe, merchants could travel more safely than before.
West of Mongolia sat the Khwarazmian Empire, a rich Muslim empire covering what's now Uzbekistan, Iran and nearby lands.
In 1218 Genghis sent a big trade caravan there. The governor of the border town of Otrar called the merchants spies and had them killed.
The Great Khan would like that governor punished. Politely asking.
Punished? No. But I'll give you a free shave.
The Shah had one envoy killed and the others' beards shaved off. That was a very, very bad idea.
In 1219, Mongol armies poured in. Within about two years, great cities like Bukhara and Samarkand had fallen.
Marco Polo later wrote that on long rides, Mongol horsemen could even drink blood from a small cut in their horse's neck. Gross, but it saved packing lunch.
The Shah died on the run, on an island in the Caspian Sea. Cities that resisted were often destroyed and their people massacred. That's the dark side of this story, and it was real.
Genghis died in 1227 while fighting in what's now northwestern China. Where is he buried? Nobody knows. Hold that thought.
His son Ögedei became the next Great Khan, the boss of all Mongols. And the conquests kept rolling.
In 1240 the Mongols captured Kyiv. Then, in April 1241, within just three days, they beat a Polish army at Legnica and a Hungarian army at Mohi.
European knights had never seen anything like it: horse archers, fake retreats, and armies moving like clockwork.
Then, in December 1241, far away in Mongolia, Ögedei died, reportedly after a night of heavy drinking.
Big news! The Great Khan is dead. The princes need to go choose the next one.
We're in the middle of Europe. Fine. Turn the army around.
Historians argue about how much Ögedei's death mattered. The army was also short on grass for its horses, and stone castles were slowing it down.
Either way, in 1242 the Mongols pulled back east, and they never pushed that far west again.
Next, Genghis's grandson Hülegü marched on Baghdad, the city of the Abbasid caliphs, the traditional leaders of the Muslim world for about five hundred years.
In February 1258 the city fell after a short siege.
Much of Baghdad was destroyed, the last caliph was killed, and a huge number of people died, at least tens of thousands.
Later writers said so many books were thrown into the river Tigris that the water ran black with ink.
Not everyone was lost, though. The Persian scientist Nasir al-Din al-Tusi went to work for Hülegü, who built him a famous observatory.
The Mongols looked unstoppable. Then, in 1260, they met the Mamluks: slave soldiers, bought as boys and trained into elite warriors, who now ruled Egypt.
Hülegü had just taken most of his army home, because another Great Khan, Möngke, had died.
At Ain Jalut, in what's now northern Israel, the Mamluks, with Baybars among the commanders, beat the Mongol force left behind.
See? They can lose. Tell everyone.
It was a huge blow. The Mongols never avenged it, and they never reached Egypt.
Meanwhile in the east, another grandson of Genghis, Kublai Khan, became Great Khan in 1260.
In 1271 he started a Chinese-style dynasty called the Yuan. By 1279 he'd conquered all of southern China, ruling from a capital where Beijing is today.
His empire ran on paper money, printed on paper made from mulberry tree bark.
Wait. You buy things with... paper? Made from trees?
Mulberry bark, stamped with my seal. And yes, everyone has to accept it.
Polo was so impressed, he joked about it.

show.text: You might say he hath the Secret of Alchemy in perfection, and you would be right!
show.who: Marco Polo on Kublai's paper money, The Travels (Henry Yule's translation)

beats.say: The catch? Later Yuan rulers printed far too much of it, and prices shot up. Remember that for later.
Kublai also wanted Japan. In 1274 and again in 1281, he sent huge fleets.
Japanese warriors fought hard on the beaches, and after the first attack they built a long stone wall along the coast.
Both times, storms hit the Mongol fleet. Historians argue the 1274 one was small, but the typhoon of 1281 was a disaster.
Even the wind is on our side!
The Japanese later called it kamikaze, meaning 'divine wind'.

show.label: The Japanese name for the storms

beats.say: But the empire was already cracking. After Möngke died, Genghis's grandsons went to war with each other.
By the time Kublai died in 1294, there were four separate khanates: the Golden Horde, the Chagatai Khanate, the Ilkhanate in Iran, and Kublai's Yuan in China.
Basically, the world's biggest family business, run by a family that couldn't stop fighting.
The Golden Horde, in today's Russia and Ukraine, collected tribute from Russian princes until 1480. That's more than two hundred years of paying the Mongols.
In China, the Yuan faced floods, famine and paper money that kept losing its value. In 1351 a massive revolt broke out, called the Red Turbans after the rebels' red headbands.
One of its leaders was Zhu Yuanzhang, a poor farmer's son who'd once been a monk and a beggar.
Your time is up, Khan. China is ours again.

tag.text: Toghon Temür, last Yuan emperor of China

beats.say: Right. I'll just... head north.
In 1368 Zhu founded the Ming dynasty, and the last Yuan emperor fled to the steppe. Mongol rule over China was over.
And Genghis's grave? It's still lost. Legend says his burial was kept secret on purpose, and no one has found it in about eight hundred years.
In 2003, scientists found one male family line in about one in twelve men across a big part of Asia. That's roughly one in two hundred men alive today.

show.label: Men worldwide carrying one family line
show.sub: about 8% across a big part of Asia (2003 study)

beats.say: They suggested it might come from Genghis and his family. Later studies questioned that, so it's a maybe.

So a boy left to starve on the steppe started an empire that linked China to Europe with roads, relay stations and passports. It was brilliant, it was brutal, and within a few generations it had split apart.
